The issue is not that Korean characters are broken in the TUI.
The problem is that Korean text inside code files edited or written by opencode gets corrupted.

Looking at the opencode source code on GitHub, it appears that files are read and written using Bun.
Since no encoding is specified, it defaults to UTF-8.

However, our existing code files are encoded in EUC-KR.
As a result, when Bun reads and writes these files using UTF-8, the Korean characters become corrupted.

This is not a TUI-related rendering issue.

Big Pickle fell off a cliff shortly after completing a successful-ish PRD for an updating core component. Whatever. Happens. Here, we are in a fresh OpenCode session, drilling down on one specific function to implement to get the ball rolling. The prompt tells OpenCode exactly where the local /dev file is that contains the exact class we are using as our precursor. I turned to the TV, and sent an email, and ten minutes later, a subtask (which is not exported), is 20 tool uses deep in attempting to find the file. It is applying find and grep patterns throughout the full scope of directories I have permissioned. (Unsettlingly, it also is asking me to allow find and grep even though "find *" and "grep *" are allowed in opencode.json.) Nonetheless, after several more greps and finds, the subtask... finds the PRD document. We are not near a context limit. Then, the agent decides to explore the _process_tasks() precursor function directly, but first runs this generated python code (for no purpose other than to list the methods of the class). I am so perplexed (pun intended) by this decision space. 1. the inspect package is deep compilation code, running on a environment python bash now. but def _process_task() is in the file. yes, these kind of checks are imperfect but plenty of code inspection tools use them too, and they are much safer. 2. where does this methods checking code come from? I strongly suggest this is a rules-based slot-fill template inside the OpenCode workflow somewhere, but is it? I need to know. Is this LLM generated code? Is this OpenCode proprietary template rules? I watched a Feng Shui guy use a 0.5 second video clip glancing out the window at a Manhattan skyline to download the exact floor plan of the apartment in the building that the videographer was asking to redecorate. Let us be real serious about what we are doing here. We are staring at the only open source viable option, too. Looking forward to sitting down at this tomorrow too. I am happy to do any PR that I am asked to explore. Thanks.

For *nix users having this issue, here's a drop-in wrapper command based on [this answer](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/5175#issuecomment-3621094440):

```bash
opencode() {
    local tmpdir="$HOME/.opencode/tmp"
    mkdir -p "$tmpdir"
    BUN_TMPDIR="$tmpdir" command opencode "$@"
}
```

> > Experienced the same issue so I did a little digging -- the systemd clue was a good one [@alhnesn](https://github.com/alhnesn). I think it's specifically systemd-journald rotating logs and causing a freeze when systemd-timesyncd is doing clock adjustments. Something is going on with the WSL time sync, I can see in my local logs there's lots of instances of `systemd-journald[50]: Time jumped backwards, rotating.` that seem to align with the cadence of freezes in the opencode tui. Pretty much exactly this issue: [microsoft/WSL#11790](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/issues/11790)
> > By running `sudo systemctl stop systemd-timesyncd` and then watching the systemd-journald logs, the journald rotations stopped... and so did the freezes in OpenCode.
> > I have no idea where this actually puts us in terms of a solution though outside of temporarily disabling timesyncd.
> 
> The time syncing was broken on my WSL on windows 11 too. I disabled the service and told wsl to use windows to sync.
> 
> You can configure it to poll much less frequently rather than disabling it entirely (WSL2 time drift is a real problem if you leave it off too long): Edit the config:
> 
> sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf.d
> sudo vim /etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf.d/poll-interval.conf
> Add:
> 
> [Time]
> PollIntervalMinSec=3600
> PollIntervalMaxSec=86400
> This sets the minimum poll to 1 hour and max to 24 hours (defaults are 32 seconds min, 34 minutes max). Then restart the service:
> 
> sudo systemctl restart systemd-timesyncd
> Alternative approach — use Windows time instead: Since WSL2 can sync from Windows, you can disable the service entirely and rely on Windows time sync. Add to /etc/wsl.conf:
> 
> [interop]
> enabled = true
> 
> [boot]
> systemd = true
> Then just leave systemd-timesyncd disabled `sudo systemctl disable systemd-timesyncd` . Windows will keep the clock reasonable. Check current status: bashtimedatectl status timedatectl timesync-status

Hi, I'd like to take this issue. Could you assign it to me?

I dug into the cause. When a subagent spawns another subagent, the child is currently using the immediate parent's session ID instead of the root parent's ID. Because of that, nested subagents don't show up in the children() list in the TUI.

I have a patch ready that adds a getRootParentID() helper so every subagent attaches under the original parent session.

>>> Alternatively, you can ignore the warnings from Windows Defender and continue using the system

Well... you can't ignore it. The DLL that triggers Windows Defender keeps changing name every time Windows Defender blocks it. It's kinda chicken & egg situation that prevents us from adding it into exclusions. You don't know the name of the DLL until you run OpenCode, and once you run it, Windows Defender blocks the file and removes it. And you can go in circles indefinitely.
